# 1. Introduction

In order to evaluate the potential insurance risk associated with a Sharknado scenario for insurance payouts for property damage purposes. A Sharknado is explained by a tornado that generates enough wind speed to be able to lift a heavy animal, such as a great white shark, out of the water and into its vortex. A Sharknado can also be called a "Shark-infested tornado".

This study starts by comparing the average great white shark to objects of similar weight, specifically cars or pickup trucks. Tornadoes are known for destroying homes and tossing around vehicles, thus finding the types of vehicles that are similar enough in weight to a great white shark makes finding the right magnitude of tornadoes required to lift a great white shark easier.

Next, finding the magnitude of a tornado capable of picking up a great white shark, or a car, is found using the EF scale (Enhanced Fujita Scale) by looking at EF ratings (@us_department_of_commerce_enhanced_nodate). The Enhanced Fujita Scale uses ratings of EF0 to EF5. Tornadoes of interest for this study are tornadoes of rating EF3 to EF5. These tornadoes have strong enough wind speeds to potentially pick up and throw cars or, in this case, a great white shark.

Finally, looking at places that are near the coast to be able to pick up a great white shark is essential to actually generating a Sharknado. There are 4 locations observed for their tornado data that fit this agenda in this study: Florida, South Carolina, Virginia, California, and Los Angeles (this is the setting of the Sharknado movie). For another comparison of tornado strength and amount, Oklahoma is also looked at for its tornado EF rating, even though it is landlocked and does not have any native shark population. These locations have tornado data taken from 2015 - 2026 using NOAA tornado data.

Combining the magnitude of tornadoes with the areas where these tornadoes touch down gives an idea of the possibility of a potential Sharknado event occurring.

# Methods

A Sharknado event involves a tornado being able to lift a great white shark out of the ocean and carry it onto land. To see if this is possible, we need to look at the physics: the weight of a great white shark, what objects are known to be picked up by tornadoes, and the magnitude of tornadoes required to pick up a shark. First, we need to find out how a great white shark could be picked up by a tornado. We will be looking at the weight of a great white shark first and comparing it to other objects that can and have been picked up by tornadoes, such as cars. Next, figuring out what strength (in EF scale from EF3 - EF5) of a tornado would be needed to be able to lift a great white shark and a car. Lastly, we are going to look at some tornadoes from 2015-2026 that are in the desired EF scale range (EF3-EF5) from 5 different places in the United States. These places are going to be Florida, South Carolina, Virginia, Oklahoma, California, and Los Angeles. These places were chosen for specific reasons. Florida has many tropical storms and is a coastal state (Florida, [-@StormEventsDatabaseFL]). South Carolina is also another place that can be hit by tropical storms and is another coastal state (South Carolina, [-@StormEventsDatabaseSC]). Virginia is a coastal state htat has had a good amount of tornadoes of our criteria (Virginia, [-@StormEventsDatabaseVA]). Oklahoma is not a coastal state, but it is the tornado capital of the United States, so we will just look at the number of tornadoes that meet our criteria (Oklahoma, [-@StormEventsDatabaseOK]). California ([-@StormEventsDatabaseCA]) was chosen because it is the state setting of Sharknado, while Los Angeles ([-@StormEventsDatabaseLA]) was picked because it is the city setting of the Sharknado movie.

Sharks and cars weigh relatively the same in pounds (lbs). The average great white shark weighs around 4,500 lbs (@fisheries_white_2025). A car SUV weighs around 3,986 lbs while a truck SUV weighs around 4,578 lbs (@noauthor_how_nodate). This means that your average great white shark weighs more than a big car and as much as a truck or SUV. We will use a car as the base to find what EF scale level will be used to lift a great white shark out of the water.

The EF scale is made up of 6 different ratings of tornado based on 3-second wind speed in mph (@us_department_of_commerce_enhanced_nodate). An EF0 tornado has the lowest wind speed, ranging between 65-85 mph, EF1 has wind speeds between 86-110 mph, EF2 has wind speeds between 111-135 mph, EF3 has wind speeds of 136-165 mph, EF4 has speeds between 166-200 mph, and EF5 has wind speeds that are over 200 mph. An EF3 tornado is likely to toss cars and trucks, while an EF4 is very likely to toss cars many feet, and an EF5 tornado is almost certain to lift and destroy cars. Since we are comparing a great white shark to the size and weight of a car SUV, and a truck SUV, that gives us a good comparison to be able to put a shark in the place of those cars in the EF scales' ability to lift cars (@quach_can_2025). We are going to look at tornadoes that are only EF3 to EF5 because those are the strength of tornadoes that are able to lift a car (@salaita_how_nodate).

# Results

The results of this study examines tornado activity over the last 10 years from specific states across the United States. Tornado strength of EF3 - EF5 is chosen due to their capabilites to lift and toss objects that are similar to sharks weight wise, these objecting being cars or trucks. The findings are shown by state and area (FL, SC, VA, CA, Los Angeles) to be able to see where and which tornadoes had the strength and location to start a Sharknado event. California and Los Angeles, CA were chosen due to being the location of the film "Sharknado".

Below is these such tornadoes being mapped on the entire United States to get an idea of where these states and their tornadoes are and why they were chosen for this study.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-plot1
#| fig-cap: "Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data Accross USA"

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)
#install.packages("maps")
library(maps)

usa_tornado <- read.csv("all_tornado_data.csv")

usa_tornado$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", usa_tornado$TOR_F_SCALE)

usa_tornado <- usa_tornado|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, BEGIN_LAT, BEGIN_LON)

usa_map <- map_data("state")

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = usa_map, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "gray90", color = "black") +
  
  geom_point(data = usa_tornado,
             aes(x = BEGIN_LON, y = BEGIN_LAT, color = TOR_F_SCALE),
             size = 2, alpha = .7)+
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
  "5" = "#2d0709",
  "4" = "#740937",
  "3" = "#da1e28",
  "2" = "#d02670",
  "1" = "#ff7eb6",
  "0" = "#ffafd2"
  ))+
  coord_fixed(1.3)+
  theme_minimal()

```

Most tornadoes happen on the eastern side of the country as shown in @fig-plot1. This gives the best ideas of where to check to see if Sharknadoes are possible. The east coast is the best place to start the search. The states that have enough tornadoes, and the states that will be examined, are Florida, South Carolina, and Virginia. 

## Results: Florida

From @fig-plot1, Florida is a place that is on the coast, so it would be possible to pick up a shark in the event of a strong enough tornado. There are enough tornadoes that touched down in Florida over the last 10 years which is a reason Florida is a state that will be analyzed.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-table1
#| fig-cap: "Florida Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data"

tornado_fl <- read.csv("fl_tornado.csv")

tornado_fl$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", tornado_fl$TOR_F_SCALE)

tornado_fl <- tornado_fl|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, BEGIN_LAT, BEGIN_LON)

tornado_fl |>
  gt()
```

@fig-table1 shows that there have been only 5 EF3 tornadoes in the last 10 years in the state of Florida. Because of an EF3 tornado being the highest EF rating, and it being "likely to toss a car or truck" we can believe that a tornado in Florida is pretty unlikely to pick up the average great white shark. Having only five EF3 tornadoes in the past 10 years seems like the chances of a Sharknado happening look pretty slim. Below is a map showing these tornadoes.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-plot2
#| fig-cap: "Florida Higher Than EF2 Tornado Map"

fl_map <- map_data("state") |>
  filter(region == "florida")

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = fl_map, 
               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),
               fill = "gray90", color = "black") +
  
  geom_point(data = tornado_fl,
             aes(x = BEGIN_LON, y = BEGIN_LAT, color = TOR_F_SCALE),
             size = 2, alpha = .7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
  "5" = "#2d0709",
  "4" = "#740937",
  "3" = "#da1e28",
  "2" = "#d02670",
  "1" = "#ff7eb6",
  "0" = "#ffafd2"
  ))+
  coord_fixed(1.3) +
  theme_minimal()
```

@fig-plot2 shows a map of Florida showing the five EF3 tornadoes that have occurred in the last 10 years. There is one tornado that shows up close to the water, but looking at the coordinates, it appears on the beach. EF3 tornadoes are likely to toss cars and trucks (@quach_can_2025). Tossing and picking up are not the same thing in this scenario, so an EF3 tornado is not very likely to fully pick up a shark.

## Results: South Carolina

A place that has similar properties to Florida, in having tropical storms frequently and being a coastal state, is South Carolina. The data below gives another place to compare to that is in an area where great white sharks are present.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-table2
#| fig-cap: "South Carolina Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data"
tornado_sc <- read.csv("tornado_SC.csv")

tornado_sc$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", tornado_sc$TOR_F_SCALE)
tornado_sc <- tornado_sc|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, BEGIN_LAT, BEGIN_LON)|>
  filter(
    TOR_F_SCALE > 2
  )

tornado_sc |>
  gt()
```

South Carolina is similar to Florida from @fig-table2. There are a lot of EF3 tornadoes with one EF4 tornado. But it's in the same boat as Florida; there has been a very limited number of powerful tornadoes over the past 10 years in South Carolina. There have been nine EF3 tornadoes and one EF4 tornado over that span. The surprising thing is that the EF4 and six of the EF3 tornadoes all happened on the same day. But the possibility of a Sharknado is very low because these tornadoes all happened away from the coast. The EF4 happened in Estill and Hampton Counties (@zotero-item-1). Below is a map showing all the tornadoes from South Carolina over the last 10 years.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

#| label: fig-plot3
#| fig-cap: "South Carolina Higher Than EF2 Tornado Map"

sc_map <- map_data("state") |>

ggplot() +

               aes(x = long, y = lat, group = group),

  "5" = "#2d0709",
  "4" = "#740937",
  "3" = "#da1e28",

  "0" = "#ffafd2"

```

The EF4 tornado is the main Sharknado threat. As seen in @fig-plot3, all tornadoes EF3 and above only appear on land and are far enough from the coast to have any real threat of a Sharknado. From the evidence from Florida and now South Carolina, a Sharknado is looking less and less possible.

## Results: Oklahoma

Oklahoma is known as the tornado capital of the United States. Tornado data from Oklahoma will give a good comparison for the amount of tornadoes that occur at the levels needed to cause a Sharknado.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-table4
#| fig-cap: "Oklahoma Higher Than EF2 Tornado Data, Ten Highest Tornadoes"
tornado_ok <- read.csv("tornado_oklahoma.csv")

tornado_ok$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", tornado_ok$TOR_F_SCALE)
tornado_ok <- tornado_ok|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, BEGIN_LAT, BEGIN_LON)|>
  filter(
    TOR_F_SCALE > 2
  )|>
  arrange(desc(TOR_F_SCALE))
tornado_ok_10 <- head(tornado_ok, n= 10)

tornado_ok_10 |>
  gt()
```

From @fig-table4, this displays only the ten highest EF scale tornadoes to hit Oklahoma because there are 27 tornadoes in the EF3 to EF5 rating. The ten highest tornadoes in Oklahoma over the last 10 years have been two EF5 tornadoes, seven EF4 tornadoes, and one EF3 tornado. This data tells that EF5s are a very rare occurrence even for the tornado capital of the country. Sharknado's would be very rare even in a place that gets strong tornadoes at the highest rate in the country.

## Results: Califorinia & Los Angeles, CA

To make a real connection to the Sharknado movie, examining the actual setting of the movie, which is California and Los Angeles, CA is the next step. The tornadoes recorded in California over the past ten years give a real idea of the possible strength of tornadoes that could hit Los Angeles, to see how it compares to the Sharknado film. The table below shows the top 10 tornadoes in EF scale strength over the last 10 years.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-table5
#| fig-cap: "California Tornado Data"

tornado_ca <- read.csv("california_tornado.csv")

tornado_ca$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", tornado_ca$TOR_F_SCALE)
tornado_ca <- tornado_ca|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, BEGIN_LAT, BEGIN_LON) |>
  arrange(desc(TOR_F_SCALE)) |>

tornado_ca_10 <- head(tornado_ca, n = 10)

tornado_ca_10 |>
```

@fig-table5 shows the 10 highest tornadoes from the last 10 years in California. There are no tornadoes that are EF3 or higher that have taken place in CA from this table. There are no tornadoes that can pick up a great white shark.

Sharknado takes place in Los Angeles, CA, as the main setting for the movie. Because of this, the table below shows only tornadoes from Los Angeles County. Los Angeles County is where the city of Los Angeles is located.


All of the tornado data over the last ten years in Los Angeles can be seen in @fig-table6. As shown, there have been only EF0 and EF1 tornadoes to hit Los Angeles over this span of time. By comparing the levels of EF ratings specified before (needing between EF3 - EF5), we can see there is not really a possibility of getting a tornado with wind speeds strong enough to pick up a shark to create a Sharknado. The mph of wind speed needed to lift a shark off the ground is about 200 mph (@salaita_how_nodate). The wind speed of an EF0 tornado is 65 - 85 mph, while an EF1 tornado has wind speeds 86 - 110 mph. This shows us that we are barely able to get to half the wind speed needed to pick a shark up off the ground in Los Angeles. ## All States

A stacked bar chart is used to see an easier comparison of all the tornadoes for each location we chose (Florida, South Carolina, Virginia, Oklahoma, California) with an EF scale rating of EF3 to EF5, and compare them to see which locations have the highest possibility of a Sharknado to occur. Note that California only has EF0 and EF1 tornadoes, so we will use those only in this chart.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-plot6
#| fig-cap: "Bar Chart for Tornadoes Higher than EF3 Over Last 10 Years for FL, SC, VA, and OK, All Tornadoes Over Last 10 Years for CA"
all_tornado <- bind_rows(
  tornado_fl,
  tornado_sc,
  tornado_va,
  tornado_ok_10,
  tornado_ca_10
)

ggplot(all_tornado, aes(x = STATE_ABBR, fill = factor(TOR_F_SCALE))) +
  geom_bar(color = "black")+
    scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Tornado Strength",
  values = c(
  "5" = "#2d0709",
  "4" = "#740937",
  "3" = "#da1e28",
  "2" = "#d02670",
  "1" = "#ff7eb6",
  "0" = "#ffafd2"
  ) ,
  labels = c("EF0","EF1","EF3","EF4","EF5")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10,by = 2)) +
  theme_minimal() #outline in black, paired color scheme
```

@fig-plot5 allows us to look at the strength of each location's tornadoes on the EF scale compared to each other. The wind speed needed to lift a shark off the ground is 200 mph (@salaita_how_nodate). An EF3 tornado has wind speeds of 136-165 mph, an EF4 tornado has speeds between 166-200 mph, and an EF5 tornado has wind speeds that are over 200 mph. This means that an EF4 or EF5 tornado is only strong enough to lift a shark off the ground. It is shown that there have only been two tornadoes in the last ten years that have been strong enough to have wind speeds of 200 mph or more. So there were only two tornadoes that were strong enough to be able to pick up a shark, but they happened in Oklahoma. That means there is no chance that there is a possibility that a Sharknado can happen in Florida, South Carolina, or Los Angeles. But in Oklahoma, there might be a possibility of a Sharknado. At the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks, OK, there is Shark Adventure, which is home to ten of the "most dangerous sharks known to man" (@noauthor_shark_nodate). These sharks are bull sharks. Jenks, OK, is in Tulsa County, so looking at  tornadoes over the last 10 years for Tulsa County, Oklahoma will give an insight into this possibility.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-table7
#| fig-cap: "Tulsa County, OK Tornado Data"
tulsa <- read.csv("tulsa_ok.csv")
tulsa$TOR_F_SCALE <- gsub("[A-Za-z]", "", tulsa$TOR_F_SCALE)
tulsa <- tulsa|>
  select(STATE_ABBR, EVENT_TYPE, TOR_F_SCALE, DAMAGE_PROPERTY_NUM)|>
  arrange(desc(TOR_F_SCALE))
tulsa <- head(tulsa, n= 10)

tulsa |>
  gt()
```

@fig-table7 shows all tornadoes that have gone through Tulsa County, Oklahoma, and shows that these tornadoes don't reach EF3 or higher at all. But Bull Sharks only weigh around 500 lbs (@noauthor_bull_nodate). This means that they are much easier for a tornado to lift up than a great white shark. An EF2 tornado has the strength to slightly move houses off their foundations and destroy mobile homes (@noauthor_weighty_2025). If an EF2 tornado went through the Oklahoma Aquarium in Jenks and destroyed the aquarium, it could potentially pick up sharks from the "most dangerous sharks known to man" exhibit to create a real-life Sharknado. Thinking of this logic, this could also apply to a lot of other aquariums throughout the country. But the chances of this happening are relatively low. The last time a tornado hit an aquarium was in 2024 when an EF1 tornado went through the Pittsburgh Zoo & Aquarium (@noauthor_pittsburgh_2024). This only resulted in little damage to the property and some trees being knocked over. This means that an EF1 tornado going through a zoo/aquarium will not cause enough damage to destroy buildings and have wind speeds strong enough to pick up objects as heavy as a shark. Thinking about the possibility of a Sharknado is pretty slim when there is a record of a tornado that went through an aquarium; there was still no chance.

Just thinking with the insurance payout possibilities in mind, storms and tornadoes that are not shark-infested will still cause property damage. Storms and tornadoes with high wind speeds and storms with varying precipitation types and amounts are still possible and can still cause massive amounts of property damage. Sharknados may be out of the picture, but there are many other ways that weather-related events can cause property damage.

# 4. Conclusion

In conclusion, this study shows that the likelihood of a Sharknado occurring is very low. By comparing the weight of a great white shark to different car types of similar weight, there is a way to determine the strength of a tornado on the EF (Enhanced Fujita) Scale, able to pick up a car (or a great white shark of similar weight). The EF rating required for this to happen is an EF3-EF5 tornado. This range of tornado strength has wind speeds of 136 mph to 200+ mph. For a Sharknado to happen, tornadoes of this strength need to happen where great white sharks are. Florida, South Carolina, Virginia, Califorina, and Los Angeles, California (chosen because it's the setting of the Sharknado movie) are coastal places. Oklahoma was also chosen to compare the amount and EF scale types with the other places mentioned. This study looks at tornado data from 2015-2026 and their strength from the EF scale.

Florida, South Carolina, and Virginia have very few tornadoes with the desired strength to be able to pick up great white sharks. Florida had just five tornadoes with an EF3 scale rating, South Carolina had nine EF3 tornadoes and one EF4 tornado, while Virginia had just five EF3 scale rating like Florida. These tornadoes all happened inland, so the possibility of picking up a great white shark is very unlikely. California and Los Angeles, California have had no tornadoes of strength EF3 or higher in the last 10 years. There will not be another Sharknado hitting LA again.

Even though Oklahoma has had many tornadoes strong enough (EF3 to EF5) to be able to pick up a great white shark over the last 10 years, there are no great whites in Oklahoma. The most likely scenario to make a Sharknado inland is having an EF3-EF5 tornado destroy an aquarium in inland places where strong enough tornadoes occur. Even then, this event is not very likely.

Overall, the insurance payouts for property damage from the event of a Sharknado are extremely unlikely, if not a zero percent chance. Tornadoes and strong storms will still exist, which is still a concern for property damage purposes.
